# Systems and Methods for Mitigating Resistor Nonlinearity Errors in a Power Converter

## Overview

The present invention provides systems and methods for mitigating resistor nonlinearity errors in a power converter. Resistor nonlinearity can introduce inaccuracies in current sensing and control, ultimately degrading the performance and efficiency of the power converter. By addressing these errors, the disclosed invention enables more precise operation and improved reliability of power conversion systems.

## Power Converter Architecture

At the core of the invention is a power converter that incorporates several key components working in coordination. The power converter includes at least one power switch coupled to an input voltage. This power switch serves as the primary element responsible for regulating the flow of power from the input source to the output.

To control the operation of the power switch, the power converter further includes a pulse width modulation (PWM) circuit. The PWM circuit generates control pulses that are supplied to the power switch, thereby governing its switching behavior. Through precise modulation of these control pulses, the PWM circuit determines the timing and duration of the power switch's on and off states, which in turn regulates the output of the converter.

## Output Inductor and Current Sensing

The power converter also comprises at least one output inductor, with each output inductor coupled to a respective power switch. The output inductor plays a critical role in storing and delivering energy as part of the power conversion process.

To monitor the current flowing through the output inductor, a current sensor is connected in parallel with the output inductor. This parallel configuration allows the current sensor to accurately measure the current characteristics associated with the inductor. In particular, the current sensor comprises at least one capacitor and at least one resistor for each output inductor. Together, the capacitor and resistor form a sensing network that provides a representation of the inductor current, enabling the converter to make informed control decisions.

The current sensor connects to the PWM circuit at a current bleed node. This connection establishes a pathway through which the sensed current information can influence the PWM circuit's generation of control pulses, thereby closing the control loop.

## Mitigation of Resistor Nonlinearity Errors

A distinguishing feature of the invention is the inclusion of at least one circuit element coupled to the current bleed node. This circuit element is configured to bleed a bleed current from the current bleed node when a power switch is turned on. By selectively drawing current from the node during the switching event, the circuit element compensates for the nonlinear behavior of the resistor within the current sensor.

Through this targeted bleeding of current, the invention effectively counteracts the errors that would otherwise arise from resistor nonlinearity. The result is a more accurate representation of the inductor current and, consequently, improved control and performance of the power converter as a whole.

# Mitigating Resistor Nonlinearity Errors in Power Converter Current Sensing

## Overview

Systems and methods are provided for mitigating resistor nonlinearity errors in a power converter. These techniques employ a current sensing arrangement that includes capacitors and resistors coupled in parallel with the output inductors of the converter, in combination with a dedicated circuit element connected to a current bleed node. The circuit element is configured to bleed current from the bleed node when a power switch is turned on, thereby reducing measurement errors and improving overall current sensing accuracy in the power converter.

## Background

Power converters commonly rely on accurate current measurements to regulate output, protect against overcurrent conditions, and maintain stable operation. One widely used approach for sensing inductor current is the DC resistance (DCR) current sensing method, in which a resistor-capacitor (RC) network is placed in parallel with the output inductor. Because the inductor possesses an inherent parasitic resistance, the voltage developed across the capacitor of the RC network ideally mirrors the current flowing through the inductor. This lossless sensing technique avoids the power dissipation associated with dedicated series sense resistors.

However, the resistors used in these sensing networks do not always behave in a perfectly linear manner. When subjected to varying voltage, current, or thermal conditions—particularly during the switching transitions of the power converter—the resistance value may deviate from its nominal value. These nonlinearities introduce errors into the sensed voltage, which in turn corrupt the current measurement. Such errors become especially pronounced during the intervals in which the power switch transitions to its conducting state, when rapid changes in voltage and current stress the sensing components.

## Description of the System

To address these challenges, the disclosed system incorporates a current sensor built around an RC network. Specifically, capacitors and resistors are coupled in parallel with the output inductors of the power converter. This parallel configuration enables the sensor to develop a voltage that is representative of the inductor current, forming the basis of the current measurement.

In addition to the conventional RC sensing components, the system introduces a circuit element connected to a current bleed node. This node represents a point within the sensing network where undesired charge or current can accumulate, particularly as a consequence of the switching activity of the power converter. The circuit element is arranged to selectively draw, or "bleed," current away from this node.

## Method of Operation

During operation, the power switch of the converter is repeatedly turned on and off as part of the normal switching cycle. When the power switch is turned on, the circuit element bleeds current from the bleed node. By removing this current at the appropriate moment in the switching cycle, the circuit element counteracts the accumulation of charge and the associated voltage distortions that would otherwise arise from resistor nonlinearity.

The timing of this bleeding action is coordinated with the switching of the power switch so that the correction is applied precisely when the nonlinearity-induced errors are most significant. As a result, the voltage sensed across the RC network more faithfully represents the true inductor current, even in the presence of nonlinear resistor behavior.

## Advantages

By actively bleeding current from the bleed node in synchronization with the power switch, the system significantly reduces the measurement errors that stem from resistor nonlinearity. This improvement in current sensing accuracy offers several benefits, including more precise current regulation, more reliable overcurrent protection, and enhanced stability of the power converter. Because the technique builds upon the widely adopted DCR sensing approach, it can be integrated into existing converter designs with minimal additional complexity while delivering a meaningful improvement in measurement fidelity.

## Conclusion

In summary, the disclosed systems and methods provide an effective solution for mitigating resistor nonlinearity errors in power converters. Through the combination of a parallel capacitor-and-resistor current sensing network and a circuit element that bleeds current from a bleed node when the power switch is turned on, the approach reduces measurement errors and improves current sensing accuracy, ultimately contributing to more robust and reliable power converter performance.

# Understanding PWM in Modern Systems

Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) has become one of the most fundamental techniques used in electronic and control **systems** today. By rapidly switching a signal between on and off states, PWM allows engineers to control the amount of power delivered to a device without significant energy loss. This makes it an essential tool in everything from motor controllers to LED dimmers and power supplies.

## The Basics of PWM

At its core, **PWM** works by varying the width of the pulses in a signal while keeping the frequency constant. The ratio of the "on" time to the total cycle time is known as the duty cycle. A 50% duty cycle means the signal is on for half the time and off for the other half, effectively delivering half the maximum power. By adjusting this duty cycle, systems can achieve precise control over output levels.

## The Role of PWM in Different Systems

**The** applications of PWM are remarkably diverse:

- **Motor Control Systems:** PWM regulates the speed of DC motors smoothly and efficiently, avoiding the heat losses associated with traditional resistive control.
- **Power Systems:** In switching regulators and inverters, PWM helps convert and manage voltage levels with high efficiency.
- **Audio Systems:** Class-D amplifiers use PWM to reproduce sound with minimal power dissipation.
- **Lighting Systems:** LED brightness is often controlled through PWM, allowing for smooth dimming without color shifts.

## Why PWM Matters

The widespread adoption of PWM comes down to efficiency and precision. Because the controlling transistors are either fully on or fully off, very little energy is wasted as heat. This is a major advantage in embedded and battery-powered systems where energy conservation is critical.

In conclusion, PWM remains a cornerstone technology across countless modern systems. The combination of simplicity, efficiency, and precise control ensures that PWM will continue to play a vital role in the design of electronic devices for years to come.

# Patent Abstract

**System and Method for Reducing Resistor Nonlinearity Errors in Power Converters**

A power converter system and method for reducing resistor nonlinearity errors in current sensing applications is disclosed. The system includes a current sensor coupled in parallel with an output inductor of a power converter, wherein the current sensor is configured to measure current flowing through the output inductor by sensing a voltage across the inductor's parasitic resistance. The system comprises a sensing network having at least one resistor and at least one capacitor arranged to match a time constant of the output inductor. A compensation circuit is coupled to the current sensor and configured to detect and correct nonlinearity errors introduced by variations in the resistance value across operating conditions, including temperature and current-dependent resistance changes. The compensation circuit applies a correction factor to the sensed current signal to produce a linearized output representative of the actual inductor current. By reducing resistor nonlinearity errors, the disclosed system provides improved current sensing accuracy without introducing additional power losses associated with dedicated series sense resistors, thereby enhancing overall converter efficiency, regulation performance, and thermal management. The system is applicable to switching regulators, DC-DC converters, and multiphase power supply architectures.

# Summary of the Invention

The present invention provides systems and methods for mitigating resistor nonlinearity in DC-DC power converters employing pulse-width modulation (PWM) control and inductor current sensing. In accordance with various embodiments, the invention addresses measurement inaccuracies arising from the nonlinear resistance characteristics of sense resistors and associated circuit elements, thereby improving the precision of current regulation and overall converter performance.

## Overview

In one aspect, the invention comprises a DC-DC power converter including a switching stage configured to convert an input voltage to a regulated output voltage under the control of a PWM controller. An inductor coupled to the switching stage carries an inductor current, and a current sensing circuit is configured to generate a sense signal representative of the inductor current. The current sensing circuit includes at least one sense resistor whose resistance exhibits nonlinear variation as a function of one or more operating parameters, including but not limited to temperature, current magnitude, and applied voltage.

## Correction Mechanism

In accordance with the invention, a compensation circuit is coupled to the current sensing circuit and configured to apply a correction to the sense signal that at least partially cancels errors introduced by the nonlinear response of the sense resistor. In certain embodiments, the compensation circuit implements a correction function derived from a characterization of the sense resistor's nonlinear behavior, wherein the correction function may be embodied as a polynomial approximation, a piecewise-linear approximation, a lookup table, or a combination thereof.

In further embodiments, the compensation circuit receives one or more operating parameter inputs—such as a temperature signal from a temperature sensor thermally coupled to the sense resistor—and adjusts the correction to the sense signal based at least in part on the measured operating parameter. The corrected sense signal is provided to the PWM controller, which regulates the switching stage in dependence upon the corrected sense signal.

## Additional Aspects

In another aspect, the invention provides a method comprising: sensing an inductor current of a DC-DC power converter to produce a sense signal; determining a correction value based on a nonlinear characteristic of a sense resistor used in sensing the inductor current; applying the correction value to the sense signal to produce a corrected sense signal; and controlling a PWM signal of the converter based on the corrected sense signal.

In some embodiments, the correction value is determined dynamically during operation of the converter. In other embodiments, calibration data representing the nonlinear characteristic is stored in a non-volatile memory during a factory calibration process and retrieved during operation. The correction may be implemented in the analog domain, in the digital domain following analog-to-digital conversion, or by a combination of analog and digital processing.

## Advantages

The disclosed techniques provide one or more of the following advantages: improved accuracy of inductor current measurement across a range of operating conditions; enhanced current-mode control stability; more precise current limiting and overcurrent protection; reduced dependence on high-precision, low-nonlinearity sense components; and improved efficiency and reliability of the power converter.

It is to be understood that both the foregoing general description and the following detailed description are exemplary and explanatory only and are not restrictive of the invention as claimed. The features described above may be combined in various configurations without departing from the scope of the invention.

# Power Converter with Capacitor-Resistor Current Sensor and Bleed Current Correction

## Overview

This circuit describes a current-sensing topology commonly used in switched-mode power converters where a **capacitor-resistor (RC) network** senses inductor current, combined with a **bleed current mechanism** to compensate for errors introduced by resistor nonlinearity.

## Core Circuit Architecture

### 1. The RC Current Sensing Network (DCR Sensing)

The fundamental technique uses the parasitic DC resistance (DCR) of the output inductor as the sensing element:

```
Inductor (L, DCR)
    ●─────/\/\/\──────●  ← Output node
    │                 │
    │    ┌────R────┐  │
    └────┤         ├──┘
         │    C    │
         └────┼────┘
           Sense voltage (Vc)
```

- The **RC filter** is placed in parallel with the inductor
- When the RC time constant matches the L/DCR time constant:
  
  $$R \cdot C = \frac{L}{DCR}$$

- The voltage across the capacitor (Vc) becomes proportional to the inductor current:
  
  $$V_C = I_L \cdot DCR$$

### 2. The Nonlinearity Problem

The sensing **resistor R** (and the DCR itself) exhibits **temperature-dependent** and **current-dependent nonlinearities**:

- Resistance drifts with self-heating
- The copper DCR has a large temperature coefficient (~3900 ppm/°C)
- These errors corrupt the current measurement, affecting current-mode control and current limiting accuracy

## The Bleed Current Correction Mechanism

### Purpose

A **bleed current** is a small, controlled current injected into or drawn from the sensing node to offset the systematic error caused by resistor nonlinearity.

### Implementation

```
        Sense node
            │
    Vc ─────●──────→ To amplifier/ADC
            │
         [Bleed 
          Current
          Source] Ib
            │
           GND
```

**Operating principle:**

1. A **correction current source (Ib)** is connected to the sense node
2. This current flows through the sensing resistor, creating a compensating voltage offset:
   
   $$V_{correction} = I_b \cdot R$$

3. The bleed current is made **proportional to a reference** that tracks the nonlinearity — for example, generated by a circuit that models the resistor's temperature or nonlinear I-V behavior

### Correction Strategy

The bleed current is engineered so that its voltage contribution **cancels the nonlinear error term**:

$$V_{sensed} = I_L \cdot DCR + \underbrace{I_b \cdot R}_{\text{cancels nonlinearity}}$$

By making **Ib track the same physical mechanism** (e.g., a matched resistor or thermal sensor generating Ib), the error and correction share a common dependency and cancel.

## Complete Signal Chain

```
┌──────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐
│  Inductor    │───→│  RC Sense   │───→│  Sense Amp   │──→ Control Loop
│  (L + DCR)   │    │  Network    │    │  (Diff)      │    (PWM/ADC)
└──────────────┘    └──────┬──────┘    └──────────────┘
                           │
                    ┌──────▼──────┐
                    │   Bleed     │
                    │  Current    │ ← Reference tracking
                    │  Source Ib  │    resistor behavior
                    └─────────────┘
```

## Design Considerations

| Aspect | Consideration |
|--------|---------------|
| **RC matching** | Precise τ matching needed; often uses trimming or auto-calibration |
| **Bleed magnitude** | Ib sized to match expected error range across operating conditions |
| **Reference generation** | Ib often derived from a matched/replica device for tracking |
| **Temperature comp.** | Combines with thermal sensing to correct DCR tempco |

## Advantages

- **Lossless sensing** — no dedicated series sense resistor (uses inductor DCR)
- **Nonlinearity correction** — bleed current actively compensates systematic errors
- **Improved accuracy** — better current-limit and current-mode control precision

---

**Note:** If you're referencing a specific patent or datasheet implementation, the exact bleed-current generation method (replica biasing, thermal feedback, digital calibration) may vary. Could you clarify the context (specific application, IC, or patent)? I can then tailor the description more precisely.

counterfactuals.output:
Happy to help with a technical abstract—though I want to flag something first, since it affects how useful my output will be to you.

I can write plausible-sounding technical prose about "a bleed current node compensating for nonlinear resistor behavior." But I don't actually know whether that specific mechanism is real, novel, or technically sound as you've described it. If I just generate confident-sounding text, I risk producing something that:

- Describes a mechanism that doesn't work the way the abstract claims
- Misuses terms of art in ways a patent examiner or your patent attorney would catch
- Invents supporting detail that isn't grounded in your actual invention

For a patent, that's genuinely risky—the abstract and specification need to accurately reflect a working invention, and fabricated technical claims can undermine the whole application.

So a few questions to make this actually useful:

1. **What's the real mechanism?** Can you describe how your bleed current node actually interacts with the resistor? (e.g., is it sourcing/sinking a compensating current, offsetting a temperature coefficient, canceling a voltage-dependent resistance term?)

2. **What nonlinearity are you correcting?** Thermal (self-heating/TCR), voltage-coefficient of resistance, current-crowding, something else?

3. **What's the sense element?** Shunt resistor, RDS(on) sensing, DCR sensing, a dedicated sense FET?

4. **What existing description do you have?** Even rough notes, a schematic description, or your inventor's disclosure would let me draft from your actual invention rather than guessing.

If you give me those, I can draft a clean, accurate abstract. And one recommendation regardless: have a patent attorney or agent review anything before filing—abstract wording can have real consequences for claim interpretation.

Want to share the underlying details?

# METHOD AND APPARATUS FOR IMPROVING CURRENT MEASUREMENT ACCURACY IN A PWM POWER CONVERTER

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

[0001] The present invention relates generally to switched-mode power conversion, and more particularly to a method and apparatus for improving the accuracy of current measurements taken at a sense node of a pulse-width-modulated (PWM) power converter during and following turn-on of a power switch.

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

[0002] In PWM power converters, it is frequently necessary to measure a current representative of the current flowing through an inductive element or a power switch. Such measurements are commonly obtained by developing a voltage across a current-sensing element, such as a sense resistor, a sense transistor, or a mirror device, and coupling the resulting signal to a sense node for evaluation by control circuitry.

[0003] A recurring difficulty arises at the instant a power switch is commanded to conduct. At turn-on, parasitic capacitances, diode reverse-recovery charge, and switching transients inject a spurious quantity of charge onto the sense node, producing a leading-edge current spike or transient perturbation superimposed upon the true sensed signal. This transient causes the measured current to deviate substantially from the actual current, degrading the accuracy of current-mode control, current limiting, and over-current protection functions.

[0004] Prior approaches have employed leading-edge blanking, in which the sense signal is simply ignored for a fixed interval following turn-on. Such blanking, however, discards valid information, introduces a minimum on-time constraint, and does not remove the perturbing charge itself, permitting residual settling errors to persist beyond the blanking interval.

[0005] Accordingly, there exists a need for a method and apparatus that actively mitigates the perturbation at the sense node upon power switch turn-on, thereby permitting earlier and more accurate current measurement.

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

[0006] In accordance with one aspect of the invention, there is provided an apparatus comprising a bleed circuit coupled to a sense node of a PWM power converter, the bleed circuit being selectively enabled in temporal association with turn-on of a power switch so as to conduct a bleed current away from the sense node, thereby removing spurious charge and accelerating settling of a sense signal toward a value representative of a true converter current.

[0007] In accordance with another aspect, a method comprises detecting or anticipating a turn-on event of a power switch, and, responsive thereto, enabling a controllably conductive path to divert current from the sense node during an interval associated with the turn-on transient, and thereafter reducing or disabling the diverted current so as not to corrupt subsequent measurement of the true current.

[0008] The bleed current may be substantially constant, time-varying, or shaped to approximate and thereby cancel the anticipated transient charge profile, and its magnitude and duration may be made programmable, adaptive, or responsive to operating conditions of the converter.

## BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS

[0009] FIG. 1 is a schematic diagram of a PWM power converter incorporating a sense node and a bleed circuit according to an embodiment of the invention.

[0010] FIG. 2 is a timing diagram illustrating a power switch drive signal, a bleed enable signal, and a resulting sense-node signal.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION

[0011] Referring to FIG. 1, a PWM power converter includes a power switch Q1 coupled to an inductive element, and a current-sensing element operatively arranged to develop a sense signal at a sense node N indicative of a current flowing in the converter. A control circuit generates a drive signal that periodically causes power switch Q1 to transition between a non-conducting state and a conducting state at a switching frequency and duty cycle determined by a PWM modulator.

[0012] A bleed circuit is coupled to sense node N. In the illustrated embodiment, the bleed circuit comprises a controllably conductive device, such as a transistor, having a first terminal coupled to sense node N and a second terminal coupled to a reference potential, and a control terminal coupled to receive a bleed enable signal. When enabled, the controllably conductive device establishes a low-impedance or current-limited path through which a bleed current I_B is conducted away from sense node N.

[0013] The bleed enable signal is generated in temporal association with turn-on of power switch Q1. As used herein, "temporal association" encompasses generation of the bleed enable signal coincident with, in advance of, or following the assertion of the drive signal that causes Q1 to conduct, and includes embodiments in which the timing of the bleed enable signal is derived from the same signal that commands turn-on of the power switch.

[0014] Referring to FIG. 2, upon assertion of the drive signal at time t0, a turn-on transient tends to inject spurious charge onto sense node N. Substantially concurrently, the bleed enable signal is asserted, causing the bleed circuit to conduct bleed current I_B and thereby to remove the spurious charge and suppress the resulting perturbation of the sense signal. At a time t1, after the transient has substantially subsided, the bleed enable signal is de-asserted or reduced, whereupon the sense signal at node N settles to a value accurately representing the true converter current, which value may then be sampled or compared by the control circuit.

[0015] In one embodiment, the magnitude of bleed current I_B is selected to approximate the average or peak spurious current injected during the turn-on transient, such that the net perturbation at sense node N is substantially cancelled. In a further embodiment, bleed current I_B is shaped over time, for example decaying from an initial value, so as to track the decaying profile of the turn-on transient.

[0016] In another embodiment, the duration during which the bleed circuit is enabled is programmable, and may be established by a timer, a one-shot circuit, a digital counter, or a comparator responsive to a state of the sense signal. The duration may further be made adaptive, being adjusted in response to one or more of input voltage, output voltage, load current, temperature, or a measured characteristic of the transient itself.

[0017] In yet another embodiment, the bleed circuit comprises a current source or current sink whose magnitude is set by a reference, and the bleed current is switched onto and off of the sense node by a switching device responsive to the bleed enable signal. In a still further embodiment, the bleed circuit is combined with a leading-edge blanking function, such that the bleed current suppresses the transient while a blanking interval, shorter than would otherwise be required, guards residual settling.

[0018] While particular embodiments have been described, it will be understood by those skilled in the art that various changes in form and detail may be made without departing from the scope of the invention. The current-sensing element may comprise a resistor, a transistor operated as a sense element, a current mirror, a transformer, or any equivalent; the power switch may comprise a MOSFET, IGBT, bipolar transistor, or other switching device; and the converter may be of buck, boost, buck-boost, flyback, forward, or any other topology.

## CLAIMS

What is claimed is:

1. A method of improving current measurement accuracy in a PWM power converter having a power switch and a sense node at which a sense signal representative of a converter current is developed, the method comprising:
   - operating the power switch to transition from a non-conducting state to a conducting state in accordance with a drive signal;
   - responsive to said transition, enabling a bleed circuit to conduct a bleed current away from the sense node so as to remove spurious charge associated with a turn-on transient of the power switch; and
   - thereafter reducing the bleed current and measuring the sense signal to obtain a value representative of the converter current.

2. The method of claim 1, wherein enabling the bleed circuit occurs in temporal association with assertion of the drive signal that causes the power switch to conduct.

3. The method of claim 1, wherein the bleed current is shaped over time to approximate a profile of the turn-on transient so as to substantially cancel a perturbation of the sense signal.

4. The method of claim 1, further comprising adjusting at least one of a magnitude and a duration of the bleed current in response to an operating condition of the converter.

5. An apparatus for a PWM power converter, comprising:
   - a current-sensing element arranged to develop, at a sense node, a sense signal representative of a converter current;
   - a power switch operable in response to a drive signal; and
   - a bleed circuit coupled to the sense node and configured to be selectively enabled in temporal association with turn-on of the power switch to conduct a bleed current away from the sense node, thereby accelerating settling of the sense signal toward a value representative of the converter current.

6. The apparatus of claim 5, wherein the bleed circuit comprises a controllably conductive device having a control terminal responsive to a bleed enable signal derived from the drive signal.

7. The apparatus of claim 5, wherein the bleed circuit comprises a current source or current sink switched onto the sense node during an interval associated with a turn-on transient of the power switch.

8. The apparatus of claim 5, further comprising a timer or comparator establishing a programmable duration during which the bleed circuit is enabled.

9. The apparatus of claim 5, wherein the bleed circuit is configured to operate in cooperation with a leading-edge blanking circuit to suppress a turn-on transient of the power switch.

10. The apparatus of claim 5, wherein a magnitude of the bleed current is adaptively established in response to at least one of input voltage, output voltage, load current, and temperature.

---
